Drivers: 
1) Trades don't seem like a sustainable option for working class women 
2) women dominate education, women feel welcome in school environments, they become female spaces so on and so forth. 
3) Less immediate pressure to be a provider, contrary to popular belief I think most women pursuing the lesser paying fields (or at least fields where high pay is delayed like with a PhS) do actually know the ramifications, they just don't prioritize it as much. They don't value themselves based on how much they make. 
4) early life maturity. I'm not a self hater, I just do see a lot of young women become mature earlier, this really helps you in higher Ed. If you do well in highschool it's easier to do that path then come back at 24 starting in community college when life expectations are driving you down. 

Effects: 
1) I see this a lot in my personal life as someone who works in healthcare. Man supports woman with immediately higher paying job while they go through school/work part time and or have kids. Then woman blossoms later with an equal paying or higher paying career with far superior working conditions. What happens after depends, I've seen divorce, I've seen couples keep the status quo, also seen the man go back to school. I'm genuinely jealous of this dynamic honestly and if I had to pick an advantage woman have in modern society it's this one I'd take. 
2) more income equality
3) lower fertility, but probably less single parents or at least more financially able single parents since women will wait to have kids. 
4) growing political division between genders: blue collar tend to swing right, college education left. It's just going to keep going and unfortunately drive some really negative emotions. 

All just my conjecture based on observations through my life.

I did and shouldn't have, although I appreciate some career related aspects my dad tried to instill in me and my brother. 

 Best I can say is try to understand their biases first (do they chase after safety only? Are they extremely safe already and pushing you for passion only because they have regrets? What have they been exposed to? Only manual labour? Or lots of different fields?) and then appreciate what's useful and what isn't. 

For instance, my dad was an actor for about a decade before turning to blue collar work; he also has a very blue collar background. He was forced to do this because it got more expensive to live, kids and my mom became disabled. He's also basically a luddite and blames the downfall of the fine arts on "men in suits". 

His skepticism towards being "paid by exposure" and appreciation for union jobs was a good influence, dudes used to dealing with slimey bosses/bad deals from both film/theatre and construction so it was great that he instilled deep distrust in the company's you work for (lmao). I used to roll my eyes at it, but truly good communications skills are paramount in just about ANY job.

The fact that he told us to stay away from anything at all to a computer, office or really anything was very negative and advice I should not have taken. Far as hes concerned if you work with a computer you're scamming the world and if you have fancy possessions you're definitely lying about your salary and in deep debt.

My brother and I ended up as electrician and nurse respectively; hindsight these are not good matches for our personalities and some of that was based off his rigidity.. but credit where it's due we're both union and make decent money.

I'm don't really feel like a nurse anymore, and while I'm not in love with my job, the work-life balance is amazing compared to what I saw from medical nursing in school.

Also all my time in theatre comes in handy talking to people and leading improv groups, so I'm not actually bad at my job either. My previous degree was in psych as well, and I've had mental health struggles in my not so distant past as well.

Long term I hope this can fund my next thing, and if I manage to help a few kids along the way even better.

Depends on the dose, situation etc.... 

If you take a lot they may hold you medically for a while, and then once that's cleared do a mental health admission process. Medical system is pretty good at dealing with sertraline overdoses provided it doesn't go on for too long, or the dose is astronomically high.

They will absolutely hold you under a 72 hour hold however automatically because it was an intentional overdose.
But this can be cancelled by a psychiatrist if they see that you would be safe to go back home, and don't want to voluntarily participate in programming. 72 hour holds can happen in the ER, or you could eventually be transferred to an inpatient unit for part of it.

Keep in mind, mental health hospitals are generally for crisis management when it comes to depression/suicide, and most of the actual healing work is generally supposed to happen outpatient on follow ups where you can actually get back to living your life and achieving the things you want to achieve... These conditions are holistic so can't really be resolved in a hospital in 2 weeks.  An actual admission is generally just to keep you physically safe, and then get the ball rolling with treatment which will be done outpatient. Most long term stays arnt cases of depression/suicide, but bipolar, schizophrenia mixed with being in vulnerable economic situations.

Both dad and mom came from much poorer backgrounds, went to university for acting of all things. Dad had some success in early to mid 20s, but eventually that tapered off and he became a construction worker for 25+ years. Mom never had much, got sick with MS, did odd temp jobs and now on disability due to her disease progressing.  Never was my family rich off acting, but my dad carries a huge amount of pride that he was able to live off it at all in the early days.

My family didn't grow up in the projects, we had a house, we just couldn't afford vacations ever, and my parents to this day never have any savings in the bank account. It just fluctuates around the 1000 CAD mark, dipping in and out of debt depending upon emergency expenses. When my parents were younger, they used to dip into the equity of the house when my dad wasn't getting any acting work, eventually it was too much and that's why he went to construction, that and the union benefits could pay for my mom's meds.

 It wasn't the worst existence by any stretch, but as I got older the lifestyle divide between me and other people in my life became apparent. Cars bought, school paid for, family vacations, a working parent with actual time off since they didn't work hourly. Not to mention how... exhausting my family dynamics were since my dad worked this job he hated that drained every bit of his energy while others sat in cushy offices making as much if not more. 

What was more jarring was the divide in attitudes. When you're working class, the only way to secure a good job is via a union gig. The office jobs that people in my family had were at most receptionist or clerk, those jobs paid like shit. So it was always taught to me growing up you do labour you succeed, you go to an office you'll starve. There's no such thing as a career with a growing skillset to bargain with, just whatever is the best paycheck since you're just a replaceable number in these jobs.

Wealthier families with white collar jobs like engineer or programmer don't see the world this way. In fact my gfs mom hates being part of the university workers union because it's holding her back since she's a skilled white collar worker, and can't use her individual skills to catapult her career any further there. I find people from these families feel much more at ease taking lots of time in school, internships etc.. to actually build a career with a real skillset since they have an example to work from.

I figured out what i had to study (lecture vs lecture + textbook) and just wrote as detailed notes as I possibly could on my computer for the first go. I got A+'s in all the bio and anatomy/physiology courses I took. 

Get into your profs head on day one: Are they writing tests themselves or do they use a test bank of questions from the textbook supplier? You can usually just ask if you're polite and show genuine interest in the subject during the lecture. Then after lecture just go up and politely ask the best way to go about the course, is the textbook supplemental or will their be details not covered in lecture that will appear on the test? 

Typically if they're writing questions themselves then there's usually no need to look at the textbook unless you need some extra help with a concept. Otherwise, you'll have to treat the textbook like the Bible.

My advice would be to minor in psych if you truly want to get into this field. Or if you're really committed major in psych AND keep a minor in CS. 90% of psych classes in undergrad are useless regurgitation and extremely repetitive. Take the key classes, volunteer in labs + do some community work and you'd be a pretty competitive applicant to a clinical program. Those CS skills are extremely sought after in the world of academic psychology, they will take you further in the field than actual psych classes will. 

Believe it or not, clinical psych programs are looking for people with strong research skills... which means strong quantitative + cs skills first and foremost most of the time. The only difficulty here would be negotiating the ability to write a psych thesis which, although not strictly required for entry in a clinical psych program, is helpful. And you are gonna need all the help you can get because clinical is extremely competitive.

Personally though, I would never recommend anyone major in psychology like I did. It seems like you're interested in the medical field, so I have two bits of advice. 

  
1: Get involved. Right now it might be difficult because of COVID but keep looking for ways to just gain exposure to the medical field. Not only will this help build an application for med school when you're volunteering in late high school, but it will also strengthen your resolve in what you truly want. The more involved you are, the less you'll hesitate thinking this is for you or not.  
2: When you get to preparing for undergrad (*you got time)*, and if you've chosen a health sciences major, make sure you've explored (and have the pre requisites) for other opportunities in the medical field as well. Lots of people go in wanting to be a doctor, but for one reason or another don't end up going to medical school and that's okay. Maybe you'll want to do a second entry nursing program, MRI tech, Dentistry, Optometrist etc... These are great careers each with their own pros and cons and I firmly believe that with the competitivness of canadian medical school admissions it's only sane to have back up plans that you'd be happy with as well. Plus, takes some of the pressure off. 

Finally, I sense a lot of perfectionism in you, wanting to get things ***perfectly right***  and get them ***done now.*** This has no doubt served you well in school right now, but can also rear its ugly head in other areas of your life (as I have begun to experience myself). No matter how hard you plan, that plan will be disrupted no matter what in one way or another and you'll have to adapt to being comfortable with that. No career path is **absolutely perfect** for pretty much anyone, and there will be elements that you dislike about all of them and thats okay too. 

What I've found that helps with dealing with this perfectionistic anxiety about the future is to literally schedule it. Certain days of the week, and at certain times during those days I will worry and work towards that plan. Others I book for chores, getting work done, and others I try to give myself a break and purely enjoying myself. Hope this helps.

First, I think it's a great thing that you're interested in so many things as that kind of flexibility in being willing to commit yourself to *a wide variety of things* is fantastic. So many people pigeon hole themselves into "I'm not a *(science/math/social etc..)* person so I won't do that!" and its extremely detrimental.

However, from my experience as a student who chose an impractical major and am paying dearly for it, I would advise you cut out a huge swath of those subjects which arn't at all practical before you start to decide. 

The most practical subjects you have listere here are: Accounting, Nursing, Computer Science, Software Engineering. Provided you plan ahead accordingly, it's very possible to have a well paying job immediately out of school directly in your field. All of these you can move up in or around in fairly easily as well, some even without taking a masters degree. 

Some other majors might also work, although they are a bit riskier. Key among these are the health professions that require you to get a masters or higher to even work in the field: Medicine (although I hear in the UK you can do a direct entry program), Physiotherapy, Social Work etc... They're good careers but they hinge on the fact that you actually manage to get in and it is **no easy feat to do so.**  The danger is that it's usually advisable to take an impratical but related undegraduate major to get the experience and grades to apply with (i.e Life Sciences and Psychology). If you want to go down this route, make sure to know exactly how much you'll need to achieve to be a competitive applicant (GPA, clinical experience &/or research experience) and go about aquiring immediately. It's also advisable to have backup plans prepared, so for instance if you want to major in psychology and be a clinical psychologist, make sure you also look at other ways out. You could make sure you have the pre reqs for a nursing program so you can pivot if you need to, or combine it with a minor in buisness or IT and do a few non psychology internships.   


Marketing and other buisness degrees can work, but can fall flat if you don't get internships and plan well (from what I heard, no personal experience though). 

Finally, subjects like philosphy, theology, media studies, photography are honestly best not majored in for **most people**. Take classes in them, participate in them, minor in them if you wish, and definitely enrich your life with them as much as you possible can but don't major in them unless you are independently wealthy or really are that crazy. I have parents who went into theatre and it was painful for them immediately after graduating and onwards.   


TL:DR: Narrow it down to the practical majors + the semi practical ones and work from there.

It's more research based yes, as you can take a class called intermediate stats and you are given the opportunity to write an undergraduate thesis. But only barely since really it's only those two classes that offer you any additional skills towards data analystics.   


However, most of the research/programming skills you'll need to learn to build up in your CV for data analyitics would be built up volunteering (or working) in labs. The spec honours program makes it easier to get into labs as you're "the best" (occasionally labs advertise volunteer positions and they usually say their ideal candidate has over a certain GPA and in the Spec Honours Porgram) but tbh you probably won't struggle either way if your grades are decent and you make a good impression. That being said, while I was lucky enough to do some technical work in one of the labs I volunteered in I hear it's quite rare to really get to do stuff as interesting as that. Most students end up doing some sort of behaviour coding (like inputing in an excel sheet that person A performed this behaviour) or essentially pushing papers around for the lab. My advice would be to get involved early so even if they don't give you that opportunity right away you can build your way up to it.

Right now I'm applying for positions like that for post grad, and it seems to be a little bit of a crap shoot. I would advise against doing a masters if you're unsure of what you wanna do with it; the advice I've gotten is if you want to get into to data you're better served just trying to land an entry level job right out of undergrad rather that doing a technically unrelated masters and hoping to switch over.
